title: Maintaining statutory certification
plain: Are all certificates up to date and tracked properly, and is the ship free of class conditions or memoranda?
why: Expired or missing certificates mean the ship may not be legally fit to trade, and open class conditions show unresolved defects.
checks: The company procedure for tracking certificate validity
A few certificates picked at random (up to five) against your tracking list
Whether any condition of class, memoranda or short-term certificate exists
That any class-related defects are in the defect reporting system
That the latest class survey results appear in the class status report
ready: Company procedure for managing certificates and supporting documents
Folders of statutory and class certificates with survey and test reports
Certificate index showing every expiry date
Class Survey Status Report (CSSR) or class status report
List of open defects from the defect reporting system
Record of class attendance in the last twelve months
traps: No clear procedure for indexing and filing certificates
Officer cannot explain how certificates are indexed and tracked
A class or flag certificate, or a supporting survey report, expired or missing
Index not kept up to date as the procedure says; class status report not available onboard
Dates in the questionnaire do not match the class report
Any condition of class, memoranda or short-term certificate
say: Our SMS has a procedure that tells us how to index, file and track every certificate. I check the index against the folders, and any survey or class finding goes into the defect system. Electronic certificates are controlled in the same way through our SMS.

practice.q: How do you make sure no certificate expires without you knowing?
a: We keep a certificate index with every expiry date
Index is reviewed as per company procedure
Surveys are planned ahead with class and company

practice.q: Do you have any conditions of class or memoranda?
a: Check the latest class status report and answer honestly
Explain that each item is in the defect system
Show the plan and dates for close-out

tip: Before the inspection, compare the class status report line by line with your certificate index so the dates match.

title: Superintendent inspection and report
plain: Did a company superintendent inspect the ship about every six months, with a full report for each visit?
why: Regular visits by shore staff give the company a true picture of the ship's condition and how onboard management is working.
checks: Inspection reports for each visit in the last eighteen months
That each report covers all operational and accessible areas
The gaps between inspections by marine and technical superintendents
That defects and weaknesses from reports were followed up to closure
Remote inspection procedure and reports, if used
ready: Full report copy for every qualifying superintendent visit in the last eighteen months
Proof defects went into the defect reporting system
Proof procedural weaknesses went into the non-conformity process
Company remote inspection procedure, if remote inspections were used
traps: A report for a declared visit is not onboard
Report format does not cover all areas of the ship; more than seven months between inspections
More than fourteen months since the last marine or technical inspection
New ship with no inspection since handover
More than one remote inspection when a physical visit was possible
Findings not followed up as defects or non-conformities
say: The company sends a marine or technical superintendent about every six months. We keep the full report from each visit onboard. Every defect goes into our defect system and procedural points go through the non-conformity process until they are closed.

practice.q: When was the last superintendent visit and what did he find?
a: Give the date and the main findings
Show the report onboard
Show how each item was followed up

practice.q: How are findings from superintendent reports tracked?
a: Defects go into the defect reporting system
Procedural issues go through non-conformity reports
Items stay open until closed with evidence

tip: Keep the last eighteen months of reports in one folder with a simple list of dates, so you can hand it over in one go.

title: Internal ISM audit
plain: Are recent internal ISM audit reports onboard, and were non-conformities closed and checked by the shore office?
why: Internal audits show whether the ship really follows its SMS, and closing findings properly stops the same problems coming back.
checks: The company procedure for scheduling and carrying out internal audits
The latest two internal audit reports under the current operator
The system that tracks non-conformities until closed
Whether the Master or a senior officer understands the audit process
ready: Company procedure for internal ISM audits with standard formats or checklists
Latest two internal audit reports
Non-conformity tracking records with time limits and close-out dates
Evidence behind each close-out, such as photos or superintendent visit notes
If the ship is new to the company, the plan for the first audit
traps: No procedure for scheduling and doing internal audits
No internal audit for more than 15 months, or over 12 months with no reason recorded
Last two audit reports not onboard; tracking records incomplete or not available to those responsible
No time limit set for corrective action; no record of the operator verifying the close-out
Non-conformity open past its time limit or closed with no evidence
Master or senior officer does not know the audit process
say: Internal audits are done at least every twelve months under a company procedure with standard checklists. Each non-conformity has a time limit, and when we finish the corrective action, the office verifies it and closes it out. Our two latest reports are here.

practice.q: How do you close out an audit non-conformity?
a: Do the corrective action within the time limit
Report completion to the company
Company verifies with evidence and records final close-out

practice.q: When is the next internal audit due?
a: Give the date from the audit programme
Twelve months maximum, up to three months more only in exceptional circumstances
Know where the schedule is kept

tip: Attach photos or the superintendent's note to every closed item. 'Done' without evidence is a common finding.

title: Master's review of the SMS
plain: Does the Master know the SMS well, and are Master's reviews done as the ISM Code and company procedure require?
why: The Master's review feeds real feedback from the ship back to the company so the SMS keeps improving.
checks: Whether the Master knows the layout of the SMS and can find things quickly
The last two Master's reviews
The company replies to those two reviews
The company procedure for the review: format, agenda, frequency, reply time
ready: The SMS in hard copy or digital form
Last two Master's reviews, fully completed
Company responses to both reviews
Company procedure for Master's review
traps: Master not familiar with the layout and contents of the SMS
Master cannot find information in the SMS quickly; no company procedure for the periodic review
Reviews not done at the frequency the procedure sets
Review not completed to the company format or agenda
Review lists no deficiencies or improvement suggestions, just ticks
Company did not reply within the set time
say: I know how our SMS is laid out and can find any procedure quickly. I do the review at least once a year using the company format, and I include real deficiencies and suggestions. Here are the last two reviews and the company replies.

practice.q: How often do you review the SMS and what do you include?
a: At least annually, whole SMS within twelve months
Deficiencies and corrective action proposals
Suggestions to improve the SMS, with input from officers and safety committee

practice.q: Show me how you find the procedure for a given task.
a: Go straight to the right section
Show you can use hard copy or digital version
No need to know every detail by heart

tip: Write specific, useful comments in your review. Inspectors can tell when it is only a tick box.

title: Structural concerns and Enhanced Survey File
plain: Is the Enhanced Survey File kept up to date, and is the hull, cargo and ballast tank coating free of structural concerns?
why: Hidden hull damage, corrosion or failed coating can lead to structural failure and pollution, so full records and a good physical condition matter.
checks: The Enhanced Survey File and whether all required sections are complete
Repair history in the last twelve months against the defect reporting system
Condition evaluation report for fair or poor coating, heavy corrosion or deep pitting
Coating Technical File for recorded repairs
Visible cracking, denting, distortion or serious wastage while walking round
ready: Enhanced Survey File, including survey reports, condition evaluation and thickness reports
Coating Technical File where required
Survey programme, main structural plans and repair history
Ship staff inspection reports for cargo, ballast and void spaces
Incident investigation reports linked to structural damage or repair
traps: No procedure to keep the Enhanced Survey File or Coating Technical File current; officer cannot explain how the file is maintained
Required surveys or reports missing from the file; ship staff inspections not recorded
Structural repair in the survey file but no defect report; structural repair after an incident with no incident investigation report
Fair or poor coating, or heavy corrosion or deep pitting, in class reports
Ballast tank coating repairs not entered in the Coating Technical File
Cracks, dents, distortion or wasted structure with no class survey
say: Our company procedure tells us how to keep the Enhanced Survey File and Coating Technical File up to date as class requires. Every repair is recorded in the file and also in our defect system. Ship staff tank inspections are recorded and kept with the file.

practice.q: What is in the Enhanced Survey File?
a: Survey, condition evaluation and thickness reports
Survey programme, structural plans, repair history
Ship staff inspections and the Coating Technical File where required

practice.q: When coating repairs are done in a ballast tank, what do you record?
a: Update the Coating Technical File
Keep it onboard for the life of the ship
Link it to the maintenance plan

tip: Cross-check the last twelve months of structural repairs in the survey file against the defect system before the inspection.

title: Structural concerns and Class Survey File
plain: Is the Class Survey File complete and current, and is the hull, hold space and ballast tank coating free of structural concerns?
why: Gas carrier structure and ballast tank coatings must be tracked closely so damage and deterioration are found and repaired early.
checks: The Class Survey File: class status reports, survey reports, repair history
Repair history in the last twelve months against the defect reporting system
Coating Technical File, where required, for recorded repairs
Survey reports for heavy corrosion, deep pitting or poor coating
Visible cracking, denting, distortion or serious wastage on the ship
ready: Class Survey File, complete and current
Coating Technical File where required
Ship staff inspection reports for cargo, ballast, hold and void spaces
Incident investigation reports relevant to structural damage and repair
traps: No procedure to keep the Survey File complete; master or Chief Engineer unfamiliar with that procedure
Survey File missing class status reports, survey reports, repair history or coating file
Coating maintenance not part of the maintenance plan; structural repair in the file but no defect report
Structural repair after an incident with no investigation report
Fair or poor ballast coating, or heavy corrosion or pitting, in reports
Visible structural damage with no occasional class survey
say: Our company procedure covers keeping the Class Survey File complete and up to date. Repairs are recorded in the file and in the defect system, and ballast coating maintenance is in our planned maintenance. Coating repairs go into the Coating Technical File where required.

practice.q: What does your Survey File contain?
a: Class status reports and survey reports
Repair history
Coating Technical File where required

practice.q: How do you handle structural damage found by the crew?
a: Enter it in the defect reporting system
Inform company and class
Record the repair in the file and investigate any incident

tip: Check that any repair you list in the Survey File also has a matching defect entry.

title: Cargo, ballast and void space inspection
plain: Are cargo, ballast and void spaces inspected on time, and are reports made in the company format?
why: Regular inspections find corrosion, coating failure and leaks before they become structural damage or pollution.
checks: The company procedure: frequencies, actions if an inspection is late, report format
Inspection reports for the full previous cycle, spot-checked against the dates declared
That each report records the detail the company form asks for
That defects found were entered into the defect reporting system
Extra inspections where class conditions, memoranda or coating condition required them
ready: Company inspection procedures and any referenced industry guidance
Inspection reports for all cargo, ballast and void spaces for the last full cycle
Open defect reports for tank structure, coatings or fittings
Communications with class about tank structure defects
Enclosed space entry permits and records for recent inspections
traps: Procedure does not give clear frequency, process and reporting criteria
Ballast or void space frequency longer than twelve months
Oil or chemical cargo tank frequency longer than thirty-six months
Any space overdue by more than a month against company period; a space left out of the inspection regime
Report form cannot record coating and structural condition by area
Defects in reports not moved to the defect system; tank structure defects not reported to class
say: Our procedure sets the frequency for each type of space. Ballast tanks, voids, pipe trunks and cofferdams are inspected yearly. Cargo tanks are inspected about every two and a half years on oil and chemical ships. Reports follow the standard form and any defect goes into the defect system.

practice.q: How often do you inspect each type of space?
a: Ballast, void, pipe trunk, cofferdam: annually
Oil and chemical cargo tanks: 2.5 years, six-month window either side
Gas carrier hold spaces: annually

practice.q: What does your inspection report record?
a: Structural deterioration, corrosion, pitting and coating condition
Leaks, equipment condition and sediment
Defects are passed to the defect system

tip: Keep a simple tracker of last and next inspection date for every space, so you can show nothing is overdue.

title: Monitoring spaces for leakage and contamination
plain: Do deck officers know how to detect leaks between cargo, bunker, ballast, void and cofferdam spaces, and are checks recorded?
why: Undetected leaks between tanks can contaminate ballast and cause oil pollution when it is discharged.
checks: Company procedures for sighting ballast surface before discharge
Sounding records for empty spaces
Ballast discharge records showing surface checks on at-risk tanks
Records of ballast line tests through cargo or fuel tanks
Whether ballast tank sighting arrangements are easy to use
ready: Procedure for sighting ballast surface before discharge
Procedure for periodic sounding of empty spaces and level checks on full tanks
Records of surface checks, soundings and level checks
Records of ballast line tests where lines pass through cargo or fuel tanks
traps: No procedure to check empty spaces for liquid coming in or to check ballast surface
Officer unfamiliar with the procedures; soundings of empty spaces not done as the procedure requires
Ballast surface not inspected before discharge from tanks next to cargo or bunker tanks
Ballast lines through cargo or fuel tanks not tested
Sighting needs many bolts removed or an enclosed space entry
Leakage in an empty space, or oil in ballast, in the last twelve months
say: Before discharging ballast from tanks next to cargo or bunker tanks, or with oil lines passing through, we sight the surface and record it. We sound empty spaces regularly and check levels in full tanks. If we find contamination or liquid migration, we follow the company procedure.

practice.q: What do you do before discharging segregated ballast?
a: Sight the surface of tanks next to cargo or bunker tanks
Also tanks with oil or hydraulic lines passing through
Record it, and follow procedure if contaminated

practice.q: How do you detect liquid moving between spaces?
a: Periodic soundings of empty spaces
Periodic level checks in full tanks
Ballast line tests where they pass through cargo or fuel tanks

tip: Make sure sighting ports can be opened quickly, because heavy hatches suggest nobody ever checks them.

title: Condition Assessment Programme (CAP)
plain: If the ship has a class CAP rating, are the dates and ratings declared correctly and the certificate available?
why: A CAP rating gives charterers an independent view of the ship's condition, so the information given must be accurate.
checks: CAP certificate against the date and module ratings declared in the questionnaire
The survey completion date, not just the certificate issue date
Any records that support the certificate
ready: CAP certificate showing survey completion date and rating for each module
Evidence of onboard survey dates if certificate shows only issue date
Supporting information or records for the certificate
traps: Information in the pre-inspection questionnaire is wrong
Rating claimed for a module still pending completion
Certificate issue date declared as the survey date
Certificate not uploaded and not onboard
say: Our CAP certificate is available onboard. The survey dates and module ratings match what the company declared. CAP is voluntary and the rating shows the ship's condition on the day of the survey.

practice.q: What does your CAP certificate cover?
a: Modules assessed and the rating for each
Dates of the onboard survey
Rating reflects condition on the survey date

tip: Check the survey completion date on the certificate. It is often different from the issue date.

title: Defect reporting system
plain: Do senior officers know how to report defects to shore, and have all defects been reported?
why: Unreported defects stay hidden from management, so repairs are delayed and risks are not controlled.
checks: The company defect procedure and how officers use it
Entries in the system: timely, sent ashore and acknowledged
A sample defect with a repair timeline and any interim measures
Any obvious defect seen during the inspection that is not in the system
ready: Company procedure for managing defects
The defect reporting system or planned maintenance system if combined
Shore acknowledgement of each defect entry
A printed list of all open defects, marking those reported to class or flag
traps: No defect reporting system or procedure
Senior officer unfamiliar with the procedure
Defects not acknowledged by shore management
Visible defects on listed or class items with no defect report
Defect that caused, or was caused by, an incident not reported as an incident
say: Under our procedure, all defects to structure, machinery, navigation, deck, cargo and electronic equipment go into the defect system. Shore management acknowledges each one and sets a repair timeline. I have printed the list of open defects for you, with class or flag notifications marked.

practice.q: What happens when you find a defect?
a: Enter it in the defect system within the company time limit
Shore acknowledges and sets a corrective timeline
Mitigating actions if safety is affected

practice.q: What if a defect caused an incident?
a: Also submit an incident report
Follow the company incident procedure
Investigation and follow-up

tip: Print the open defect list before the inspector arrives and walk the deck and engine room yourself looking for defects that are not on it.

title: Defect reporting to class, flag and others
plain: When defects exist, did the company tell class, flag or the port as needed, and were short-term certificates or waivers issued?
why: Defects that affect class or statutory equipment must be disclosed so the ship is not trading without proper approval.
checks: Class status report for conditions of class, memoranda or short-term certificates
Open defects that should have been reported to class or flag
Pre-arrival notices where a short-term certificate or waiver applies
That any conditions set by class or flag were complied with
ready: Company procedure for notifying class, flag and other parties
Class status report
Defect system with a printed list of open defects, class and flag reports marked
Shore messages saying the defects were assessed and what was reported
Class or flag letters with mitigating conditions, and port pre-arrival notices
traps: No procedure for shore to decide if class, flag or others must be told
Senior officers do not know the procedure
Significant open defect with no proof that class or flag were informed
Class or flag conditions imposed but no evidence they were met
say: Under our procedure, shore management assesses each defect to decide who must be told: class, flag or the port. For any short-term certificate or waiver, we follow the conditions set and keep the messages onboard. Port pre-arrival notices are made when required.

practice.q: Who decides if class or flag must be informed of a defect?
a: Shore management evaluates under company procedure
Procedure says what, when and by whom
Records of notifications are kept onboard

practice.q: What do you do if flag gives a waiver with conditions?
a: Follow every condition
Keep the records
Inform the port of arrival if required

tip: Keep all class and flag correspondence for a defect in one folder next to the defect entry.

title: Management of change
plain: Is the company Management of Change procedure followed for changes to class or statutory structure, machinery and equipment?
why: Unplanned changes to the ship can create new risks, so each one needs approval, risk assessment and updated documents.
checks: The company MOC procedure
Changes declared in the last twelve months in the pre-inspection questionnaire
The MOC register or index onboard
The request, risk assessment and documents for any recent change
Any recent change you can see on board that was not declared
ready: Company MOC procedure
MOC register or database index
MOC request form for every change in the last twelve months
Supporting papers: risk assessments, training plans, updated drawing lists
traps: No MOC procedure for class or flag regulated changes
Senior officer cannot explain the MOC process
A change in the last twelve months not declared in the questionnaire
A change made with no approved MOC form and supporting documents onboard
say: Our MOC procedure says which changes need approval and which, like for like replacement, are excluded. Each change has a request, shore approval, risk assessment and updates to affected drawings and procedures. All of them are indexed in our MOC register.

practice.q: What counts as a change that needs MOC?
a: Changes to structure, machinery or equipment under class or statutory rules
New installations or modifications
Like for like replacement is usually excluded

practice.q: What happens after a change is approved?
a: Tell the people affected
Update drawings, manuals and checklists
Confirm updates are done and file the records

tip: Walk round before the inspection looking for anything new or modified, and check each one has an MOC file.

title: Ballast Water Management Plan
plain: Do officers know the Ballast Water Management Plan, and do records show ballast was handled as the plan says?
why: Ballast water can spread harmful organisms and, if mishandled, can also stress the hull or pollute.
checks: The approved Ballast Water Management Plan and the BWM Certificate
Ballast water record book entries against the plan
Cargo and ballast plans and records of ballast timings
The exchange plan with stresses, draughts and trim, if exchange was done
Messages to flag and port if the treatment plant failed
ready: Ship-specific approved BWM Plan in the working language
International Ballast Water Management Certificate
Ballast Water Record Book, up to date
Recent cargo and ballast plans
Exchange sequence plan showing stresses, if exchange was done
Notifications and replies if treatment could not be used
traps: No plan or no valid certificate
Plan not approved by flag or class, or not ship specific
Responsible officer does not know the plan
Plan not in the working language of the ship; record book not kept to company procedure
No sequential exchange plan with longitudinal stress
Ballast treatment plant defective in any way; treatment plant bypassed against the plan
say: Our plan is ship specific and approved, and the BWM Certificate shows our main method. We record every ballast operation in the record book. If the treatment plant fails, we inform flag and port and follow any conditions they give.

practice.q: Who is responsible for the plan and what must they know?
a: The officer named in the plan
Contents of the plan and record book entries
What to do if the plan cannot be followed

practice.q: What if the ballast treatment plant breaks down?
a: Follow company procedure
Tell flag and port state
Comply with any conditions they impose

tip: Check your record book entries against cargo and ballast plan times. Mismatches stand out quickly.

title: VOC Management Plan
plain: Do officers know the VOC Management Plan, and are its steps to reduce VOC emissions followed and recorded?
why: Crude oil cargo releases harmful vapour, so the plan aims to keep emissions as low as practical.
checks: The VOC Management Plan
Records of cargo operations and tank pressures during the voyage
That the cargo plan includes the plan's requirements
VOC training records
The target tank pressure shown in the cargo control room
ready: Approved ship-specific VOC Management Plan in a language the officers understand
Training records for the plan
Records of loading, carriage, discharge and crude oil washing as the plan requires
Current cargo plan
Deck logbook
traps: Plan not approved or not ship specific; plan not in a language the Master and officers understand
Responsible person does not know the plan
Accompanying officer unaware of what the plan needs during current cargo operation
No evidence of training or of procedures used
Target operating pressure not shown in the cargo control room
Tank pressure kept well below target by venting to atmosphere
say: Our VOC plan names the person responsible and sets a target tank pressure, which is displayed in the cargo control room. We follow it for loading, carriage, discharge and crude oil washing, and keep the required records. The cargo plan includes the plan's requirements.

practice.q: What is the target pressure for the cargo tanks?
a: State the value from the plan
Explain it is kept as high as safely possible
If venting is needed, lower the pressure as little as possible

practice.q: What does the plan ask you to do on this operation?
a: Follow the loading and carriage steps in the cargo plan
Keep the required records
Consider crude oil washing effects

tip: Put the target pressure on a clear label in the cargo control room and quote it from memory.

title: Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP)
plain: Do the Master and senior officers know the SEEMP, and have its energy saving and fuel reporting steps been carried out?
why: The SEEMP cuts fuel use and emissions, and fuel data must be collected and reported correctly each year.
checks: The SEEMP, Part I and Part II
Evidence that the Part I energy saving measures were carried out or monitored
Records of fuel data collection, aggregation and reporting
Statement of Compliance for fuel oil consumption reporting
Whether the Master or Chief Engineer knows the plan
ready: Ship-specific SEEMP
Logbook evidence of measures: voyage planning, speed, trim, hull maintenance
Annual fuel consumption, distance and hours underway records
Evidence of reporting to the flag administration
Statement of Compliance - Fuel Oil Consumption Reporting (5,000 GT and above)
traps: Master or Chief Engineer does not know the SEEMP; part I has no ship-specific package of measures
No evidence the measures were carried out or monitored
Part II does not describe how fuel data is collected and reported
No Statement of Compliance issued
Fuel records leave out boilers, inert gas generator or other consumers
Fuel records not split by fuel type
say: Our SEEMP Part I lists ship-specific measures such as voyage planning, weather routeing, speed and trim, and hull maintenance. Part II describes how we collect, total and report fuel use for all consumers. We keep the records and have the Statement of Compliance.

practice.q: Which fuel consumers are included in your records?
a: Main and auxiliary engines, boilers, inert gas generator, any others
Each fuel type recorded separately
Counted whether underway or not

practice.q: What energy saving measures do you apply?
a: Name the measures in the SEEMP Part I
Show how they are applied and monitored
Point to the log entries that prove it

tip: Make sure the Chief Engineer and Master can both name three or four SEEMP measures and where the proof is kept.

title: SMS content available to all crew
plain: Can everyone onboard easily get the SMS content they need, in a language they understand?
why: A procedure nobody can find or read does not protect anyone.
checks: The SMS manuals in hard copy or electronic form
Evidence that changes to the SMS were told to the right people
Easy access to navigation procedures on the bridge
Versions of checklists and procedures in use
A random rating: can they find and understand the SMS relevant to them
ready: SMS manuals, current and relevant to this ship
Records of SMS changes being communicated and understood
Navigation procedures on the bridge, with backup power if electronic only
Enough hard copies, or workstations and training for electronic access
traps: Manual hard to navigate or slow to use
Large parts not relevant to the ship, such as other ship types
Too few hard copies in the right places; electronic only, but not everyone has access or training
Navigation procedures not on the bridge, or electronic with no backup power
Old copies not updated, or old checklists still in use
A rating cannot access or understand the SMS part for their job
say: Our SMS is available to everyone in a language they understand, and the navigation procedures are on the bridge. When the SMS changes, we brief the crew and keep a record. Old copies are removed so only current versions are in use.

practice.q: How do you tell the crew about a change in the SMS?
a: Brief the people affected promptly
Make sure they understand
Keep a record

practice.q: (To a rating) Where do you find the procedure for your job?
a: Know the way to access it
Be able to read it in your language
Ask your supervisor if unsure

tip: Check every checklist copy has the same revision number as the SMS before the inspector arrives.

title: Authority and lines of communication, including the DPA
plain: Does the SMS show clear authority and communication lines, and does everyone know their own and who the DPA is?
why: In an emergency or a safety concern, people must know who decides and who to call ashore.
checks: The SMS chart or text showing authority and communication lines
A senior officer: do they know key shore contacts including the DPA
A junior officer or rating: do they know who the DPA is, how to reach them and what the role is
ready: SMS section on authority and communication lines, charts or flowcharts are fine
DPA name and contact details displayed or given to all
List of key shore contacts for navigation and technical matters
traps: SMS does not clearly show authority and communication lines
Senior officer unfamiliar with key shore contacts
Junior officer or rating does not know who the DPA is, contact details or role
say: Our SMS shows the chain of authority from Master to officers to ratings and the company, with the Master's overriding authority on safety. Everyone onboard knows the DPA's name, contact and role. Senior officers also know the superintendent and navigation contacts ashore.

practice.q: Who is the DPA and how do you contact them?
a: Give the name and role
Know the contact details or where they are posted
Explain the DPA is the link between ship and company

practice.q: Who do you report to and who reports to you?
a: Describe your place in the SMS chart
Know the next level above and below
Know when to go to the Master or shore

tip: Make sure every rating, not only officers, can say the DPA's name without looking it up.

title: HVPQ accurately completed
plain: Does the company's vessel questionnaire (HVPQ) in the SIRE database correctly describe the ship?
why: The inspection is built partly from the HVPQ, so wrong data misleads inspectors and charterers.
checks: The inspector reviews the HVPQ before boarding against uploaded certificates
Sections such as general information, certificates, crew, navigation, structure and propulsion
Anything that looks inconsistent with the ship type
Any errors or gaps are raised with the Master
ready: Certificates and documents matching what the HVPQ says
Class status report and crew matrix
Notes of any recent changes to the ship or crew
traps: Several errors or omissions in ownership, class status, certificate validity or outfitting
HVPQ not updated before the inspection
say: The company updates the HVPQ before each inspection. If you find something that does not match the ship, I will check it with you now and tell the office. Our certificates onboard match the details declared.

practice.q: The HVPQ says something different from what you see. Why?
a: Check the facts honestly
Confirm what is correct
Report the difference to the company to correct

tip: Read the HVPQ once yourself before the inspection and mark anything that no longer matches the ship.

title: Last Port State Control inspection
plain: Are records of the last PSC inspection onboard, and were any deficiencies fixed and closed out per company procedure?
why: PSC findings show what outside inspectors found, and closing them out shows the company acts on problems.
checks: The company procedure for managing PSC inspections
PSC reports for the last three years, or the last one if none in that time
Proof that deficiencies were corrected and closed with shore approval
That the most recent report matches what was declared and uploaded
ready: Company PSC procedure
All PSC reports for the previous three years
Defect or non-conformity records showing close-out of each deficiency with shore approval
traps: No company procedure for PSC inspections
Most recent PSC report not uploaded to the OCIMF repository within five days, if used
Onboard reports missing the most recent PSC inspection shown in MoU databases
No documented close-out of deficiencies with shore approval
PSC data in the questionnaire is wrong in any respect
say: Our company procedure covers how we manage a PSC inspection and close deficiencies. Every PSC report for the last three years is here. Each deficiency is recorded in our defect or non-conformity system and closed with shore approval.

practice.q: How were the deficiencies from the last PSC inspection closed?
a: Entered into defect or non-conformity system
Corrected and evidence recorded
Closed with shore management approval

tip: Staple the close-out evidence to each deficiency in the PSC report so you can show it in seconds.

title: Crew qualifications and officer matrix
plain: Are officers and ratings properly qualified, and does the online officer matrix match who is onboard?
why: Only properly trained and certified people should run a tanker and its cargo.
checks: Matrix details against certificates of competency, endorsements and sea service for a sample of officers
Advanced tanker training for senior officers, junior deck officers and cargo or gas engineers
Basic tanker training for junior engineers and a deck rating
Advanced training for any rating with immediate cargo responsibility, such as the pumpman
English standard of officers, as heard during the inspection
